content: Appropriate prevention services, such as voluntary medical male circumcision in priority countries within sub-Saharan Africa or harm reduction services for individuals who use drugs, should be made available. Individuals are encouraged to undergo retesting at a later time to ensure accurate diagnosis and follow-up. A variety of HIV testing and counseling models are available to enhance access to HIV diagnosis. These include testing services within healthcare facilities, standalone sites, and numerous community-based approaches. These models are comprehensively detailed in the WHO 2012 strategic HIV testing and counseling framework. The use of rapid HIV diagnostic tests at the point of care has become a critical strategy to expand access, provide same-day results, and facilitate timely referral and follow-up. Countries should adopt a strategic mix of service delivery models tailored to their local context, the nature of the epidemic, cost-effectiveness, and available resources. This approach aims to diagnose individuals living with HIV as early as possible, enabling timely linkage to antiretroviral therapy (ART). A single HIV test is insufficient for diagnosis; confirmation must follow the steps outlined in the updated WHO 2012 HIV testing strategies (algorithms). Quality assurance systems must be implemented to minimize false-positive and false-negative results. Failure to ensure this can lead to incorrect test results, with potentially severe long-term consequences. WHO recommends routine provider-initiated HIV testing and counseling in clinical settings as an efficient and effective method to identify individuals with HIV who could benefit from treatment. All forms of HIV testing and counseling must be voluntary and adhere to the five C’s: consent, confidentiality, counseling, correct test results, and connection to care, treatment, and prevention services. Coerced or mandatory testing is never appropriate, regardless of the source of coercion. Individuals undergoing HIV testing and counseling must provide informed consent, which can be verbal, and should be informed of the testing process and their right to decline. Confidentiality must be maintained, ensuring that discussions between the provider and the individual are not disclosed without explicit consent. However, confidentiality should not reinforce secrecy, stigma, or shame. Counselors should discuss with individuals whom they may wish to inform and how this can be done. Shared confidentiality with trusted partners, family members, or healthcare providers can often be beneficial. HIV testing and counseling services must include high-quality pre-test information and post-test counseling. Quality assurance mechanisms, supportive supervision, and mentoring systems should be in place to ensure the provision of high-quality counseling and accurate test results. Quality assurance may involve both internal and external measures, with support from national reference laboratories as needed. Connections to prevention, care, and treatment services should include effective referral to appropriate follow-up services, including long-term prevention and treatment support. Quality assurance of both testing and counseling is essential across all approaches. In generalized epidemics, provider-initiated testing and counseling should be recommended for all individuals attending healthcare facilities, including adults, adolescents, and children, across various settings such as medical and surgical services, sexually transmitted infection clinics, hepatitis and TB clinics, public and private facilities, inpatient and outpatient settings, mobile or outreach services, antenatal care, family planning, maternal and child health services, and services for key populations. In concentrated and low-level epidemics, provider-initiated testing and counseling should be recommended for individuals presenting with clinical signs or conditions indicative of HIV infection, including TB, as well as HIV-exposed children and symptomatic infants. It should also be considered in settings such as sexually transmitted infection clinics, hepatitis services, antenatal care, and services for key populations, including men who have sex with men, transgender individuals, sex workers, and people who inject drugs. Community-based HIV testing and counseling, linked to prevention, care, and treatment services, is recommended in addition to provider-initiated testing and counseling. This approach is particularly important in reaching individuals earlier in the course of HIV infection and populations that may not typically access healthcare services. Rapid HIV diagnostic tests using finger-prick blood samples, administered by trained lay counselors and community health workers, have facilitated the expansion of testing in community settings, including homes, transport stations, religious facilities, schools, universities, workplaces, and venues frequented by key populations. Community-based testing should complement facility-based testing to achieve universal knowledge of HIV status and earlier diagnosis linked to care and treatment. This includes mobile, door-to-door, index, campaign, workplace, and school-based testing approaches. Evidence suggests that community-based approaches increase first-time testing rates and identify individuals with higher CD4 counts, although facility-based testing often yields higher rates of positive results. Couples HIV testing and counseling is acceptable, feasible, and effective. It identifies seroconcordant positive couples who can be linked to treatment and receive adherence support, as well as serodiscordant couples who can benefit from prevention interventions. These services should be offered to married, cohabiting, premarital, and polygamous couples, as well as other partnerships. Couples testing should always be voluntary, and providers must be aware of the potential for intimate partner violence, supporting individuals who do not wish to test with their partners. HIV-exposed infants and children under 18 months should be tested within four to six weeks of birth to enable early initiation of ART if infected. Virological testing is required for definitive diagnosis in this population due to the persistence of maternal HIV antibodies. Early testing, prompt return of results, and rapid treatment initiation are critical, as untreated infants face high mortality rates in the first year of life. Point-of-care virological testing, currently in development, is expected to improve early diagnosis and treatment. Provider-initiated testing and counseling for pregnant women, with linkage to prevention and care, is essential to promote maternal health and prevent new pediatric infections. Retesting during the third trimester, labor, or shortly after delivery is recommended due to the high risk of acquiring HIV during pregnancy. Many countries prioritize provider-initiated testing in antenatal care as part of their strategy to eliminate mother-to-child transmission of HIV, often bundling HIV testing with other relevant tests and strengthening maternal and child health systems.
